findings.problem: The screen an audience reaches when the link is turned off is the only screen in the product that is factually wrong, and the only one that speaks in a fault register. "The day was Saturday 3 October 2026." is hardcoded past tense with no reference to the clock, so a link switched off in July tells the couple's family that the most important day of their life is over. The headline "This link has stopped working." names a malfunction, and it contradicts the promise the owner was given one screen earlier on publish — "Anyone holding it then sees that it has ended" — so one state carries two names and the product ships the harsher one. It then spends its third sentence walking the alarm back, repeating "stopped working" a second time in four lines: "Nothing has been deleted. Only the link stopped working." Three sentences, and two of them exist to undo the damage the first one did.
findings.fix: Headline becomes "This link has ended." — the word publish already uses for this state. Body branches on the clock through the accessor already in the file: where daysFrom(F.today, F.project.primaryDate.date) > 0 render "The day is " + F.fmt.longYear(...) + ". Ask " + F.workspace.owner + " for a new link."; at 0 or below keep "The day was ". Third line becomes "Nothing has been deleted." — delete the clause "Only the link stopped working."

findings.element: .b-todayRule and .b-tick[data-lead="true"] on owner-flight, owner-editing, phone and desk; the publish state, which carries no accent at all
findings.problem: The language's own rule is one accent per screen, spent on the thing that is happening, and "two accents on one screen means neither is one". Driven and measured across the state matrix, four of the highest-traffic surfaces paint two indigo objects: the hairline under the hero, meaning today, and the lead tick on the rail, meaning the nearest thing ahead. Indigo therefore carries two different meanings simultaneously — on the phone they sit about 130px apart — and neither reads as the one. Meanwhile publish, the screen the whole owner journey climbs to and the moment the plan becomes theirs, contains no indigo anywhere; nor does unfurl, nor ended. The accent is being obeyed rather than spent: it is paying for a 1px divider and a 6px dot, and never once for an event.
findings.fix: Demote the divider — .b-todayRule { background: var(--fore-16); } — nothing is lost, because the line directly beneath it already says "Today is 16 July" in words. That leaves .b-tick[data-lead="true"] as the single accent on every approach surface and .b-dayNow as the single accent on the morning. Spend the freed accent once on publish: .b-linkField { border-color: var(--accent); } so the live link is the accented object on the one screen where something is actually happening.

findings.element: .b-todayLabel in horizon() (render-b.js:125) against the rail's today marker (render-b.js:180); on print, .b-unit plus the same marker plus the footer stamp
findings.problem: Every surface that draws the measure states today twice, in two grammars, both visible at once and about 700px apart at 1440: "TODAY IS 16 JULY" on the left, "Today, 16 July" on the right. The renderer's own comment claims paper was exempted from exactly this defect, but the printed keepsake is the worst case of it — the sheet dates itself three times, "79 days away on Thursday 16 July 2026", "Today, Thursday 16 July 2026" and "Updated 15 July 2026", twice for the same day in two forms. The owner surface adds a fourth grammar for a single instant: "Live since 15 July" in the share line and "Updated 15 July 2026" in the footer are the same timestamp printed two ways on one page. Each instance is small; together they are the signature of strings written per component rather than edited as one document.
findings.fix: Delete the .b-todayLabel node from horizon() at every medium — states.loading builds its own copy inline and keeps it, so the unanchored-time rule still holds where there is no rail. The rail marker at the head of the measure becomes the single statement of today, and it already sits where the reading starts. On print, render that marker as "Today" alone, since the unit line beneath the count already carries the dated form. In foot(), print the stamp through F.fmt.medium as "Updated 15 July", and pass stamp:false on the owner surface, where "Live since 15 July" already states that instant.

findings.problem: One cancelled moment is described four ways inside one block. The row says "Not going ahead". Folded, the owner reads "One thing is not going ahead" and a guest reads "The city hotel shortlist is not going ahead". Open the disclosure — one press later, same reader — and both become "One of them did not happen", which changes tense from present to past and changes noun from "one thing" to "one of them". On the printed sheet and on the wedding morning both forms are on the page simultaneously, twelve pixels apart: "City hotel shortlist — Not going ahead" immediately above "One of them did not happen." A comment in the file records that this sentence was moved to close the block so the morning would not end on a cancelled hotel search; with the disclosure opened it does exactly that — the last two lines before the footer on the keepsake screen are the failure and a gloss on the failure.
findings.fix: Delete the dropped.length ? h("p.b-behindNote", { "data-when": listed ? "listed" : "open", text: "…did not happen." }) node entirely. Wherever the rows are visible — print, the day, the open disclosure — the row's own "Not going ahead" is the statement and needs no gloss. Keep only the folded summary, and give both reader variants the row's own words: append " One is not going ahead." for the owner and " The city hotel shortlist is not going ahead." for the guest, so the block never uses a second tense for this fact.

findings.element: the state after Set the day in states["owner-empty"] — .b-emptyBody, the "Add a moment" action, #b-empty-hint (render-b.js:1254-1262, 1246)
findings.problem: The first screen a new owner reaches after setting the day gives the same instruction three times inside about 130 vertical pixels: the prose "Nothing sits between today and the day yet. Everything you add is measured from it.", the button "Add a moment", and the status line "The day is set. Moments come next." The prose is also a near-repeat of the sentence on the screen immediately before it — "Everything on this page is measured from it, so it is the only thing needed to start." — so the product's second sentence to a brand-new owner is its first sentence again, and "The day is set." restates at 15px what the 148px count and the ceremonial date directly above have already said at full volume. This is the empty-state class the defect library names: one first move, offered once.
findings.fix: Let the button be the instruction. Trim .b-emptyBody in this state to its first sentence, "Nothing sits between today and the day yet.", and clear #b-empty-hint after the surface re-renders — it is role="status", so "The day is set. Moments come next." is still announced once and then leaves no residue on screen.

biggestWin: One grammar for distance, held intact all the way through: the same number, unit and sentence shape carry from the 148px hero to the rail figure to the accessible name to the unfurl card to the printed sheet, and the plural lives in exactly one function so "1 days" cannot happen. Around it sits a set of limit and refusal messages most shipped software never gets near — "This is as far as it goes. Wedding day is the last day.", "This is as near as it goes. Tomorrow is the soonest.", "That day has gone. Pick one still ahead.", "That is not a date. Try 3 October 2026." — each stating a boundary as a fact and handing back the next move, with no apology, no exclamation, no jargon and no blame. The honesty devices match that standard: "Nothing to preview yet" as inert text rather than a dead button, "days away when this was sent" on a card that genuinely cannot update, "The plan has not been deleted, and the link still works" on a slow load, and "It carries the day, the distance and the plan, and nothing else: no notes, no suppliers, no prices." on publish. "When is the day?" as the first thing an empty project says is the whole product in four words. This voice is already premium, already restrained, and already fit for Home, Notes and Tasks to inherit. What stands between it and 9.5 is one editorial pass over the string table with two rules enforced — one statement per fact per surface, and one tense per state — plus one small decision about what indigo is allowed to mean. That is polish measured in hours, not a build and not a different direction.
